pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You search for help with git and get a blog post, a YouTube video, and git-scm.com. Which is official, how can you tell, and why does the difference matter?
expected_points: official docs are published and maintained by the tool's makers, on the project's own site or shipped with the tool (man pages, --help)
recognizable by the domain / who maintains it, e.g. git-scm.com for git, go.dev for Go
unofficial content can rot (written for old versions) or be wrong with nothing forcing a correction
learn anywhere, but verify facts against the official reference

questions.prompt: Take an error like `cat: recipes.txt: No such file or directory` — what are the parts of a typical error message, and how does a stack trace extend them?
expected_points: who is speaking (the program), what went wrong (the message), and where (file/line or the thing involved)
a stack trace is the breadcrumb trail of function calls that led to the failure
look first at the deepest frame that is your own code

questions.prompt: What goes into a good question about a problem, and what surprising thing often happens while writing one?
expected_points: what you were trying to do, what you expected, what actually happened, what you already tried
exact error text copy-pasted, never paraphrased
a minimal example: smallest steps that reproduce the problem
writing the question often reveals the answer (rubber-duck effect)

questions.prompt: Three situations: you're brand new to a tool; you need what one specific flag does; a guide's commands don't match what your version does. Which kind of documentation fits each, and why?
expected_points: new to a tool: tutorial (teaches by doing, no need to know what to ask)
one exact fact: reference, e.g. a man page (complete and precise)
version mismatch: changelog / release notes (what changed between versions)
name the question first, then pick the document

questions.prompt: A tool prints fifteen errors at once. How many do you try to fix before running it again, and why?
expected_points: only the first one
one mistake cascades into follow-on errors that may not be real
fix, re-run, repeat

questions.prompt: You're about to paste an error message into a search engine. What two edits make the search work better?
expected_points: put the exact message in quotes
strip parts specific to you (your file names and paths) so it matches other people's version of the same error
